A person who has it reads the temperature profile, sees flooding or weeping coming and brings the column back without going off specification.
skills.learned: On the job at a chemical plant or refinery; process technology (PTEC) associate degree programs.

skills.name: Distributed Control System Operation
skills.what: Running a continuous or batch plant from the control room: watching the unit through its control system, moving setpoints, answering alarms and directing the operators outside. A person who has it keeps the unit steady through an upset, knows which alarm matters first and takes the plant to a safe state when it must.
skills.learned: Years as an outside operator on the same unit, then board training on a simulator and beside a qualified board operator.

skills.name: Aircraft Turbine Engine Maintenance
skills.what: Inspecting, servicing and repairing a turbine engine installed on or removed from an aircraft. A person who has it can find a fault from engine indications and change the modules and accessories the manual allows.
skills.learned: Military aircraft powerplant schools and qualification on the engine; an FAA Part 147 school and the powerplant rating of the FAA mechanic certificate. Engine makers run type courses.

skills.name: Aircraft Engine Removal and Installation
skills.what: Taking an engine off an aircraft and putting one on: disconnects, hoisting, mounts, rigging and leak checks. A person who has it can change an engine and ready it for its ground run.
skills.learned: Military aircraft maintenance schools; FAA Airframe and Powerplant training; on the job on the aircraft type.

skills.name: Aircraft Fuel System Maintenance
skills.what: Finding and repairing faults in aircraft fuel tanks, cells, pumps, valves and plumbing. A person who has it can open a tank safely, repair a leak and return the system to service.
skills.learned: Military aircraft fuel systems schools; FAA Airframe and Powerplant training. Tank entry takes the employer's confined space and fuel cell qualification.

skills.name: Aircraft Electrical System Troubleshooting
skills.what: Tracing faults in aircraft power generation, distribution, lighting and control circuits. A person who has it can isolate a fault with the wiring diagram and repair or replace the part.
skills.learned: Military aircraft electrician schools; FAA Airframe and Powerplant training; on the job.

skills.name: Aircraft Environmental System Maintenance
skills.what: Servicing cabin pressurization, air conditioning and anti-ice systems. A person who has it can test the system, find the leak or failed valve and restore it.
skills.learned: Military aircraft electrical and environmental systems schools; FAA Airframe and Powerplant training; on the job on the aircraft type.

skills.name: Helicopter Rotor and Drive System Maintenance
skills.what: Maintaining rotor heads, blades, transmissions and drive shafts, including track and balance. A person who has it can change a dynamic component and bring vibration within limits.
skills.learned: Military helicopter repairer schools; FAA Airframe and Powerplant training, then the helicopter maker's course. Track and balance is learned on the job.

skills.name: Propeller Maintenance
skills.what: Inspecting, servicing, removing and balancing aircraft propellers. A person who has it can change a propeller and set its controls.
skills.learned: Military aircraft propulsion schools; FAA powerplant training. Major repair is done at an FAA propeller repair station.

skills.name: Egress System Maintenance
skills.what: Removing, inspecting and installing ejection seats, canopies and their explosive devices. A person who has it can make a seat safe, service it and certify it armed.
skills.learned: Military egress and aircrew escape systems schools, with explosives safety certification; the seat makers' courses.
tools: Seat safety pins and maintenance stands

skills.name: Aircraft Phase Inspection
skills.what: Carrying out the scheduled inspection of an aircraft by its work cards and writing up what is found. A person who has it can open, inspect and close an inspection zone to the manual.
skills.learned: Military aircraft maintenance schools and on the job in an inspection crew; FAA Airframe and Powerplant training. A civil aircraft's annual inspection is signed by a mechanic with inspection authorization.

skills.name: Ground Support Equipment Maintenance
skills.what: Repairing the carts that power, cool, lift and service aircraft on the ground. A person who has it can fault-find a power cart, hydraulic test stand or air start unit.
skills.learned: Military ground support equipment schools; diesel, hydraulic and electrical programs, then on the job at an airline, airport or ground handler.

skills.name: Unmanned Aircraft System Maintenance
skills.what: Servicing an unmanned aircraft, its payloads, ground control station and data links. A person who has it can turn the system around between flights and replace failed units.
skills.learned: Military unmanned aircraft repairer schools; the maker's courses on the system; on the job.

skills.name: Diesel Engine Maintenance
skills.what: Servicing and repairing diesel engines: fuel, air, cooling and lubrication systems, injectors and valve adjustment. A person who has it can keep an engine in service and fix its common faults.
skills.learned: Diesel technology programs at community colleges and trade schools; military mechanic and engineman schools; on the job. ASE certifies diesel engine technicians (test T2).

skills.name: Diesel Engine Overhaul
skills.what: Tearing a diesel engine down, measuring its parts, fitting new ones and testing it. A person who has it can rebuild an engine to specification.
skills.learned: On the job in a rebuild shop, dealer or shipyard after diesel training; military engine overhaul courses. Engine makers certify their dealers' technicians.

skills.name: Marine Gas Turbine Maintenance
skills.what: Operating, inspecting and repairing gas turbines that drive ships and generators. A person who has it can run the plant, borescope the engine and change its accessories.
skills.learned: Navy gas turbine systems technician schools and watch qualification; the engine maker's courses. Civilian work is at shipyards, power plants and pipeline stations.

skills.name: Steam Plant Operation
skills.what: Running the steam side of a ship or power plant: turbines, condensers and the feed and condensate systems that return water to the boiler or steam generator. A person who has it can warm up, roll, operate and secure a turbine plant and hold it within limits.
skills.learned: Navy machinist's mate and nuclear power schools and watch qualification; maritime academies; on the job at a power plant. Some states and cities license stationary engineers.

skills.name: Generator Set Maintenance
skills.what: Maintaining an engine-driven generator: the engine, the alternator, its controls and protection. A person who has it can service a set and find why it will not start or hold load.
skills.learned: Military power generation schools; diesel and electrical programs; on the job with a generator dealer. The Electrical Generating Systems Association certifies generator technicians.

skills.name: Valve Maintenance and Repair
skills.what: Taking valves apart, lapping seats, repacking and testing them. A person who has it can restore a leaking or stuck valve.
skills.learned: On the job aboard ship or in a shipyard, power plant or valve shop; pipefitter and millwright apprenticeships. Shops that repair relief valves hold the National Board's VR authorization.

skills.name: Reduction Gear Maintenance
skills.what: Inspecting and maintaining main reduction gears, bearings and shafting. A person who has it can read tooth contact and bearing wear and say what must be done.
skills.learned: On the job in a ship's engineering department or a shipyard; gear makers' field service training.

skills.name: Steering and Suspension Repair
skills.what: Repairing the steering and suspension of trucks and other wheeled vehicles: steering gear and linkage, springs, shock absorbers, axles, wheel bearings and alignment. A person who has it can find why a vehicle wanders, pulls or wears its tires and put it right to the manual.
skills.learned: Automotive and diesel technology programs; military wheeled vehicle mechanic schools; on the job. ASE tests it (T5 for trucks, A4 for cars).

skills.name: Tracked Vehicle Maintenance
skills.what: Repairing tracked vehicles: track, suspension, final drives and power packs. A person who has it can change a power pack and keep track and suspension in service.
skills.learned: Army and Marine Corps tracked vehicle repairer schools; on the job at a depot or with a vehicle maker. Equipment dealers teach the same undercarriage work.

skills.name: Vehicle Drivetrain Repair
skills.what: Repairing what carries power from a vehicle's engine to its wheels or tracks: clutches, transmissions, transfer cases, axles and drive shafts. A person who has it can remove, repair and refit a drivetrain assembly.
skills.learned: Diesel and automotive technology programs; military vehicle mechanic schools; on the job. ASE tests it (T3 for trucks).

skills.name: Brake System Repair
skills.what: Repairing hydraulic and air brake systems. A person who has it can inspect, rebuild and bleed a brake system.
skills.learned: Diesel and automotive technology programs; military vehicle mechanic schools; on the job. ASE tests it (T4 for trucks); 49 CFR 396.25 sets who may inspect a commercial vehicle's brakes.

skills.name: Vehicle Electrical Diagnostics
skills.what: Finding faults in vehicle starting, charging, lighting and electronic control circuits. A person who has it can trace a fault with a meter and the wiring diagram.
skills.learned: Automotive and diesel technology programs; military vehicle mechanic schools; on the job. ASE tests it (T6 for trucks, A6 for cars).

skills.name: Heavy Equipment Maintenance
skills.what: Repairing dozers, loaders, cranes and excavators: undercarriage, booms, buckets and blades and the hydraulics that work them. A person who has it can keep earthmoving and lifting equipment working.
skills.learned: Diesel and heavy equipment programs, many run with dealers; operating engineers' apprenticeships; military construction equipment repairer schools.

skills.name: Turret and Fire Control Maintenance
skills.what: Maintaining a combat vehicle turret: its drives, stabilization, sights and firing circuits. A person who has it can fault-find the turret and bring the sights into alignment.
skills.learned: Army and Marine Corps tank, fighting vehicle and artillery maintainer schools; on the job at a depot or with the vehicle maker.

skills.name: Generator Paralleling and Load Control
skills.what: Bringing generators on line, paralleling them and sharing load. A person who has it can run a plant of several generators without dropping the load.
skills.learned: Navy electrician's mate and military power plant operator schools, then watch qualification; on the job at a power plant or data center.

skills.name: Switchgear Maintenance
skills.what: Inspecting, cleaning and testing switchboards, breakers and protective relays. A person who has it can rack out, service and test a breaker.
skills.learned: Electrical apprenticeships and military electrician schools; on the job with a utility or testing company. The InterNational Electrical Testing Association certifies test technicians.

skills.name: Medium Voltage Distribution
skills.what: Building and maintaining power distribution above 600 volts: cables, transformers and terminations. A person who has it can switch, ground and work a medium voltage circuit safely.
skills.learned: Lineworker and electrical apprenticeships; military power distribution schools. Done under the employer's qualified-person rules, built on OSHA 1910.269 and NFPA 70E.

skills.name: Battery and UPS Maintenance
skills.what: Servicing storage batteries and uninterruptible power supplies. A person who has it can test capacity, replace cells and keep the system ready.
skills.learned: Military electrician schools; battery and UPS makers' service courses; on the job at a utility, telephone exchange or data center.

skills.name: Motor Rewinding
skills.what: Stripping and rewinding the coils of motors and generators and testing the result. A person who has it can return a burnt-out motor to service.
skills.learned: On the job in a motor repair shop; the Navy's rewind course for electrician's mates. The Electrical Apparatus Service Association trains to its repair standard, AR100.

skills.name: Refrigeration System Repair
skills.what: Finding leaks, recovering and charging refrigerant and replacing compressors and controls. A person who has it can restore a refrigeration or air conditioning plant.
skills.learned: HVAC and refrigeration programs and apprenticeships; military utilities schools. Opening a refrigerant circuit takes EPA Section 608 certification.

skills.name: Boiler Operation
skills.what: Lighting off, running and securing a boiler and treating its water. A person who has it can hold steam pressure safely and test the safeties.
skills.learned: On the job under a licensed operator; stationary engineer apprenticeships; military utilities schools. Many states and cities license boiler operators by examination.

skills.name: Water Treatment System Operation
skills.what: Running the equipment that purifies, softens or treats water, and testing the product. A person who has it can keep water within specification.
skills.learned: Water technology programs at community colleges; military water treatment schools; on the job. States certify the operators of public water systems.

skills.name: Radar System Maintenance
skills.what: Aligning, testing and repairing radar transmitters, receivers, antennas and displays. A person who has it can find the failed unit from the symptoms and restore performance.
skills.learned: Military electronics schools for the system; an electronics technology degree; on the job. Repairing marine radar takes the FCC radiotelephone license with the ship radar endorsement.

skills.name: Sonar System Maintenance
skills.what: Testing and repairing sonar transmitters, receivers, arrays and processors. A person who has it can isolate a fault to a unit or hydrophone and replace it.
skills.learned: Navy sonar technician schools and on the job aboard ship; civilian work is at Navy maintenance centers, shipyards and the systems' makers.

skills.name: Radio Communication System Maintenance
skills.what: Aligning and repairing radios, satellite terminals and their antennas. A person who has it can test a set against its specification and fix what fails.
skills.learned: Military electronics schools; electronics technology programs; on the job. Repairing aviation and marine transmitters takes the FCC General Radiotelephone Operator License.

skills.name: Antenna and Waveguide Installation
skills.what: Installing, pressurizing and testing antennas, transmission lines and waveguide. A person who has it can put up an antenna system and prove its match.
skills.learned: Military electronics schools and on the job with an installation team; employers' tower climbing and rigging training.

skills.name: Electronic Warfare System Maintenance
skills.what: Maintaining receivers, jammers and countermeasures dispensers. A person who has it can test the system against simulated signals and repair it.
skills.learned: Military avionics and electronic warfare schools, which need a security clearance; on the job at a depot or with the system's maker.

skills.name: Weapon Control System Maintenance
skills.what: Maintaining the computers, consoles and interfaces that aim and fire weapons. A person who has it can run the system tests and trace a fault through it.
skills.learned: Military fire control schools for the system; on the job at a depot, shipyard or the system's maker.

skills.name: Inertial Navigation System Maintenance
skills.what: Aligning and repairing gyrocompasses and inertial navigators. A person who has it can align the system and replace failed assemblies.
skills.learned: Military avionics and navigation equipment schools; avionics programs; the maker's courses at a repair station or depot.

skills.name: Avionics Line Troubleshooting
skills.what: Finding which avionics unit has failed on the aircraft and replacing it. A person who has it can work a fault from the pilot report to the box using built-in test and the wiring diagram.
skills.learned: Military avionics schools and on the job on the flight line; avionics programs. Civilian credentials are the NCATT Aircraft Electronics Technician certification and the FCC radiotelephone license.

skills.name: Automatic Test Equipment Operation
skills.what: Running automated test stations to test and fault-isolate electronic assemblies. A person who has it can load a test program, connect the unit and act on the result.
skills.learned: Military avionics test station schools; electronics technology programs; on the job at a depot, repair station or electronics plant.

skills.name: Cryptographic Equipment Maintenance
skills.what: Testing and repairing secure communications equipment and handling it to its rules. A person who has it can restore a secure circuit.
skills.learned: Military communications security maintenance courses, open only with a security clearance; on the job for the government or a cleared contractor.

skills.name: Biomedical Equipment Repair
skills.what: Installing, calibrating and repairing medical equipment such as monitors, imaging and laboratory analyzers. A person who has it can return a device to service and document it safe.
skills.learned: Biomedical equipment technology associate programs; the military's biomedical equipment technician school; on the job. The AAMI Credentials Institute's CBET is the technician credential.

skills.name: Munitions Assembly
skills.what: Building up bombs, rockets, mines and other munitions from their components and fuzing them. A person who has it can assemble a munition to its technical order and test its firing circuit.
skills.learned: Military munitions and ordnance schools, with explosives safety certification; on the job at an ammunition plant or depot.

skills.name: Munitions Serviceability Inspection
skills.what: Inspecting ammunition and explosives for condition and serviceability and keeping their records. A person who has it can sentence a lot as serviceable or not.
skills.learned: Military ammunition schools and on the job; the Army trains civilian ammunition surveillance specialists in a career program of its own.

skills.name: Aircraft Weapons Loading
skills.what: Loading and unloading munitions on aircraft and checking the stations. A person who has it can lead a load to its checklist.
skills.learned: Military aircraft armament and aviation ordnance schools, then load crew certification on each aircraft and weapon, renewed on a schedule.

skills.name: Weapons Release System Testing
skills.what: Testing the racks, launchers and circuits that carry and release weapons. A person who has it can prove a station will release and find why one will not.
skills.learned: Military aircraft armament and aviation ordnance schools; on the job at a depot or an aircraft maker.

skills.name: Gun System Maintenance
skills.what: Disassembling, inspecting and repairing gun systems and their feed and drive mechanisms. A person who has it can time and gauge a gun and return it to service.
skills.learned: Military armament, gunner's mate and artillery repairer schools; on the job at an arsenal, depot or gun maker.

skills.name: Small Arms Repair
skills.what: Inspecting, gauging and repairing rifles, pistols and machine guns. A person who has it can find the worn part and replace it.
skills.learned: Military small arms repairer schools; gunsmithing programs at community colleges and trade schools; makers' armorer courses.

skills.name: Missile System Maintenance
skills.what: Testing, handling and maintaining guided missiles and their support equipment. A person who has it can test a missile, read the result and replace sections.
skills.learned: Military missile maintenance schools for the system, with explosives safety certification; on the job at a depot or the missile's maker.

skills.name: Torpedo Maintenance
skills.what: Preparing, testing and overhauling torpedoes. A person who has it can turn a torpedo around from recovery to ready.
skills.learned: Navy torpedo maintenance schools; on the job at a Navy undersea weapons facility or with the torpedo's maker.

skills.name: Launcher System Maintenance
skills.what: Maintaining missile, rocket and torpedo launchers: their mechanical, hydraulic and electrical parts. A person who has it can test a launcher and repair it.
skills.learned: Military gunner's mate, missile and launcher repairer schools for the system; on the job at a shipyard, depot or the launcher's maker.

skills.name: Nuclear Weapons Maintenance
skills.what: Inspecting, maintaining and handling nuclear weapons under two-person control. A person who has it can carry out a maintenance procedure exactly as written.
skills.learned: Taught only in the services and at the Department of Energy's weapons plants, to people certified under a personnel reliability program.

skills.name: Industrial Sewing
skills.what: Running industrial sewing machines to make and repair fabric and webbing items. A person who has it can sew a seam to a specified stitch and strength.
skills.learned: On the job at a cut-and-sew plant or canvas shop; military aircrew survival equipment and parachute rigger schools.

skills.name: Survival Equipment Inspection
skills.what: Inspecting and repacking life rafts, life preservers, helmets and survival kits on their schedule. A person who has it can certify an item ready for use.
skills.learned: Military aircrew survival and flight equipment schools; on the job at an FAA repair station. Parachutes are packed by FAA certificated parachute riggers.
tools: Raft and vest leak test rigs

skills.name: Oxygen Equipment Servicing
skills.what: Testing and servicing oxygen masks, regulators and converters. A person who has it can test a regulator and keep oxygen equipment clean.
skills.learned: Military aircrew survival and flight equipment schools; on the job at an FAA repair station, with oxygen cleanliness training.

skills.name: Pipe Fitting and Layout
skills.what: Measuring, cutting, bending and fitting pipe to a drawing. A person who has it can make up a piping run and prove its fit before joining.
skills.learned: Pipefitter apprenticeships, shipyard apprentice schools and Navy schools; pipefitting programs at trade schools. NCCER certifies pipefitters.

skills.name: Carbon Arc Gouging
skills.what: Removing metal and weld defects with a carbon arc and compressed air. A person who has it can back-gouge a weld or cut out a defect cleanly.
skills.learned: Welding programs and shipyard welding schools, beside stick welding; on the job.

skills.name: Stud Welding
skills.what: Welding studs and fasteners to plate with a stud gun. A person who has it can set the gun and prove the weld by bend test.
skills.learned: On the job, with the equipment maker's training; shipyard and structural welding schools. Qualified by the bend tests in AWS D1.1.

skills.name: Reactor Plant Operation
skills.what: Operating a nuclear reactor and its control systems within its limits. A person who has it can start up, operate and shut down the plant by procedure.
skills.learned: The Navy's nuclear power school and prototype training, then watch qualification. A commercial plant's operators hold a Nuclear Regulatory Commission license.

skills.name: Radiological Controls
skills.what: Surveying for radiation and contamination and controlling work so exposure stays low. A person who has it can survey an area, post it and control a job in it.
skills.learned: Navy nuclear and engineering laboratory technician training; radiation protection programs at community colleges; on the job. The National Registry of Radiation Protection Technologists registers technicians.

skills.name: Plant Water Chemistry Control
skills.what: Sampling and analyzing plant water and adding chemicals to hold it in specification. A person who has it can keep a steam or reactor plant from corroding.
skills.learned: Navy engineering laboratory technician training; chemistry technician programs; on the job in a power plant's laboratory.

skills.name: Reactor Instrumentation Maintenance
skills.what: Calibrating and repairing the instruments that measure and protect a reactor. A person who has it can test a protection channel and restore it.
skills.learned: The Navy's nuclear power school and prototype training; instrumentation programs, then a nuclear plant's own training for instrument and control technicians.

skills.name: Fuel Quality Testing
skills.what: Sampling fuel and testing it for water, sediment and specification. A person who has it can say whether fuel is fit to use.
skills.learned: Military fuels and petroleum laboratory schools; on the job at a refinery, terminal or airport fuel farm. The tests are ASTM methods.

skills.name: Liquid Oxygen and Nitrogen Production
skills.what: Running the plant that liquefies air and separates it into oxygen and nitrogen, storing the product and testing its purity. A person who has it can start the plant, hold it in production, fill storage and transfer tanks and sample the product.
skills.learned: Military cryogenics schools; on the job at an industrial gas company's air separation plant, with its cryogenic and oxygen safety training.

skills.name: Polymer Material Testing
skills.what: Testing plastic resin, rubber compound and molded specimens for the properties a lot is released on: melt flow, density and moisture of resin; Mooney viscosity, cure curve and hardness of rubber; tensile, elongation and impact of molded bars. A person who has it prepares and conditions specimens to the ASTM method, runs the instrument and knows whether a lot is in specification.
skills.learned: On the job in resin, compound and plastics laboratories, and in chemical technology programs.
tools: Rubber process analyzers and Mooney viscometers

skills.name: Textile Testing
skills.what: Testing yarn and fabric to standard methods: yarn count, twist and evenness; fabric weight, construction, tensile, tear and burst strength, abrasion and pilling; dimensional change after laundering; and colorfastness to washing, crocking and light. A person who has it conditions samples, runs each test to its ASTM or AATCC method and reports a result the customer will accept.
skills.learned: On the job in a mill's quality laboratory; the methods are published by ASTM and the American Association of Textile Chemists and Colorists.

skills.name: Charpy Impact Testing
skills.what: Measuring the energy a notched specimen absorbs when a pendulum breaks it at a set temperature. A person who has it checks the notch, brings the specimens to temperature, breaks each within seconds of leaving the bath, and reports lateral expansion and percent shear as well as energy.
skills.learned: On the job in a materials laboratory, to ASTM E23.

skills.name: Failure Analysis of Materials
skills.what: Finding out why a part broke, cracked, corroded or wore: reading the fracture surface, sectioning through the origin, and checking chemistry, hardness and microstructure against the specification. A person who has it preserves the evidence, names the failure mode (overload, fatigue, stress corrosion, embrittlement) and writes the report that says what to change.
skills.learned: A materials or metallurgy degree and time in a failure analysis laboratory.

skills.name: Scanning Electron Microscopy
skills.what: Imaging a surface at high magnification with an electron beam and reading its chemistry with the X-ray detector. A person who has it prepares and mounts the sample, sets beam and detector for the question asked, and reads fracture features, coatings, particles and element maps from the result.
skills.learned: Taught on the instrument in a university or company laboratory; the instruments' makers give operator courses.

skills.name: Material Qualification
skills.what: Proving a new material, process or supplier fit for production: planning the tests, running the lots and coupons, comparing the results with the requirement and writing the qualification report. A person who has it decides what must be shown before a material is released for use, and what change would call for showing it again.
skills.learned: Learned on the job in materials and processes engineering, to the customer's or the industry's qualification standards.

skills.name: Material and Process Specification Writing
skills.what: Writing the specification a material or a special process is bought and run to: composition and condition, process limits, tests, acceptance criteria and what the supplier must record. A person who has it turns test data and industry standards into requirements a supplier and an inspector can both be held to, and keeps the approved materials list in step with them.
skills.learned: Learned on the job in a materials and processes group, working from the industry's own specifications (SAE AMS, ASTM, NASA).

skills.name: Hot-Dip Galvanizing
skills.what: Coating steel with zinc by dipping it in a molten bath: cleaning in caustic, pickling in acid, fluxing, dipping and withdrawing at the right rate, quenching, and checking coating thickness and finish. A person who has it hangs work so it drains and vents, keeps the kettle's temperature and chemistry right, and never sends a wet or sealed part into the zinc.
skills.learned: On the job in a galvanizing plant. The American Galvanizers Association's process seminar trains plant staff as Master Galvanizers.

skills.name: Finish Sanding
skills.what: Sanding wood parts and assemblies for finish, and between coats, by hand and with orbital and profile sanders. A person who has it works through the grits in order, keeps edges and profiles crisp, removes scratches and glue without sanding through veneer, and scuff-sands a sealer coat without cutting through it.
skills.learned: On the job in the first weeks in a finishing room or furniture plant.

skills.name: Flatline Finishing
skills.what: Running the automatic line that finishes flat panels and doors: sanding, spray or roll coating, flash-off, and UV or oven curing. A person who has it sets coat weight, line speed and lamp power, checks cure and film build, and keeps the line clean through color changes.
skills.learned: On the job in a cabinet, door or panel plant; line makers train operators.

skills.name: Wood Finish Touch-Up and Repair
skills.what: Repairing dents, scratches and finish defects in finished wood so they cannot be seen: filling with wax, fill sticks or burn-in resins, re-graining with markers and toners, and blending the sheen. A person who has it repairs at the plant's final inspection or a customer's site without refinishing the whole piece.
skills.learned: On the job; finishing suppliers' touch-up courses.

skills.name: Wood Staining and Glazing
skills.what: Developing a wood finish's color: spraying or wiping stains, applying toners, glazes and highlights, and evening out sapwood and grain. A person who has it matches a finish to a master panel across different woods and lots, and knows how each coat affects the next.
skills.learned: On the job in a furniture or cabinet finishing room; coating suppliers train finishers.

skills.name: Digital Press Operation
skills.what: Running a toner, liquid electrophotographic or inkjet production press from its print queue: loading stock, calibrating color, running variable data and keeping the press within its color tolerance. A person who has it works the RIP and the job file as well as the press, and swaps consumables and clears faults without losing a run.
skills.learned: On the job; press makers train operators.

skills.name: Flexographic Press Operation
skills.what: Running a narrow-web or wide-web flexographic press on labels, film, paper or board: mounting plate cylinders or sleeves, choosing anilox rolls, setting impression and web tension, and drying or curing the inks. A person who has it controls ink viscosity and pH, holds register and color through the run, and solves dot gain, pinholing and dirty print.
skills.learned: On the job; the Flexographic Technical Association's FIRST Press Operator certification (levels 1 to 3).
tools: Central impression, stack and in-line flexo presses

skills.name: Offset Press Operation
skills.what: Running a sheetfed or web offset press: hanging plates, setting the feeder and delivery, the ink and dampening, and bringing color and register to the approved proof. A person who has it keeps the ink-water balance through the run, washes blankets and rollers, and changes over to the next job quickly.
skills.learned: Graphic communications programs at high schools and community colleges, and on the job from press helper to lead operator.

skills.name: Screen Printing
skills.what: Printing through a stencil on a mesh screen onto garments, signs or parts, on a manual or automatic press. A person who has it coats and exposes screens, sets off-contact, squeegee pressure and angle, registers the colors and cures the ink.
skills.learned: On the job in a screen printing shop; industry association workshops.

skills.name: Press Color Control
skills.what: Holding printed color to a standard by measurement: reading density, dot gain and color difference from the sheet or web with a spectrodensitometer, adjusting ink keys, anilox and plates, and running the press to a published method such as G7 or FIRST. A person who has it brings a press to the proof by numbers, not by eye alone, and fingerprints a press so prepress can compensate for it.
skills.learned: Years on press; G7 Professional and G7 Expert certification from PRINTING United Alliance's Idealliance; the FTA's FIRST certification.

skills.name: Computer-to-Plate Imaging
skills.what: Imaging and processing offset printing plates on a platesetter. A person who has it calibrates plate curves, runs and maintains the processor or a processless workflow, checks plates for dot reproduction and defects, and has the plate at the press when it is needed.
skills.learned: On the job in prepress; platesetter makers train operators.

skills.name: Flexographic Plate Making and Mounting
skills.what: Making photopolymer flexographic plates (imaging the mask, UV exposure, solvent, thermal or water processing, drying and finishing) and mounting them on cylinders or sleeves with the right tape. A person who has it holds relief depth and dot reproduction, applies distortion for the cylinder, and mounts plates in register.
skills.learned: On the job in a plate department or trade shop; the FTA's FIRST Prepress Operator certification.
tools: Solvent, thermal and water plate processors

skills.name: Preflight and Imposition
skills.what: Checking a customer's files before they go to plate (fonts, images, color space, bleed, trapping and dielines), then imposing pages or labels onto the press sheet or web. A person who has it catches the file that would print wrong, and lays out signatures, step-and-repeat and marks for the press and the bindery.
skills.learned: Graphic communications programs; on the job in a prepress department.

skills.name: Proofing and Color Management
skills.what: Making the proof a customer signs and the press must match: building and applying ICC profiles and press curves, calibrating proofers and monitors, and verifying proofs against a standard. A person who has it ties prepress, proof and press to one color target, and can explain a color difference to a customer.
skills.learned: Graphic communications programs and on the job; G7 Professional and G7 Expert certification.

skills.name: Gelcoat Spraying
skills.what: Spraying gelcoat into a waxed and released mold to the thickness the part needs: catalyzing to the shop's temperature, holding the gun's distance and pattern, checking wet-film thickness and knowing when the coat is ready to laminate over. A person who has it leaves no runs, thin spots or porosity in the finished surface.
skills.learned: On the job at boat, RV cap and bath plants; spray equipment makers train on their guns; covered by the American Composites Manufacturers Association's Certified Composites Technician credential.
tools: Gelcoat spray guns with catalyst injection

skills.name: Spray-Up Lamination
skills.what: Building a fiberglass laminate by chopper gun: spraying chopped glass and catalyzed resin into the mold to thickness, laying in woven reinforcement and core where the schedule calls for them, and rolling out the air before it gels. A person who has it holds thickness and glass content by eye and by gauge.
skills.learned: On the job at boat, RV cap and bath plants; covered by the American Composites Manufacturers Association's Certified Composites Technician credential.

skills.name: Yarn Piecing and Knotting
skills.what: Joining broken yarn ends and new packages by hand or with a splicer: weaver's knots, fisherman's knots and air splices that pass through guides, needles and reeds. A person who has it pieces up an end without holding the machine longer than it must and leaves a join that does not show in the yarn or fabric.
skills.learned: On the job, in the first days in a spinning, weaving or knitting mill.

skills.name: Fiber Opening and Carding
skills.what: Running the line that turns baled fiber into a clean, even sliver: laying down bales to the blend plan, feeding openers and blenders, and tending cards and draw frames. A person who has it holds sliver weight and evenness, watches for neps and trash and stops a card that starts to load.
skills.learned: On the job in a yarn mill.

skills.name: Yarn Spinning
skills.what: Tending frames that draft and twist sliver or roving into yarn by ring, rotor (open-end) or air-jet spinning: piecing ends, creeling roving, doffing full packages and cleaning. A person who has it patrols a set of frames, keeps ends-down low and spots the position making weak or off-count yarn.
skills.learned: On the job in a yarn mill.
tools: Ring, rotor and air-jet spinning frames

skills.name: Yarn Winding and Twisting
skills.what: Winding yarn from bobbins onto cones and packages and twisting or plying singles together on automatic winders and twisters. A person who has it sets tension and package density, keeps clearers and splicers cutting and joining as they should, and makes packages that run off cleanly at the next mill.
skills.learned: On the job in a yarn, thread or weaving mill.

skills.name: Braiding Machine Operation
skills.what: Running braiders that interlace strands of yarn, wire or fiber into rope, cord, sleeving, hose reinforcement or catheter shafts: loading carriers, setting pick count and tension, and splicing broken strands. A person who has it holds braid angle and diameter along the run and stops for a broken or slack carrier.
skills.learned: On the job at a rope, narrow fabric, hose, wire and cable or medical tubing plant.

skills.name: Knitting Machine Operation
skills.what: Running circular, flat, warp or hosiery knitting machines: creeling yarn, threading feeders, mending holes and needle lines, doffing rolls or bags of goods, and checking stitch and weight. A person who has it stops a machine at the first drop stitch or press-off and can tell a needle fault from a yarn fault.
skills.learned: On the job in a knitting mill.

skills.name: Loom Operation
skills.what: Running a set of weaving machines: repairing warp and filling breaks, restarting without a start mark, changing filling packages and watching the cloth for defects as it is woven. A person who has it keeps many looms running at once and knows which stops are the weaver's to clear and which are the fixer's.
skills.learned: On the job in a weaving mill; a weaver trains on a few looms for weeks before taking a full set.
tools: Air-jet, rapier, projectile and water-jet looms

skills.name: Nonwoven Line Operation
skills.what: Running a line that forms fabric straight from fiber or polymer without yarn: spunbond and meltblown, or carding with needlepunch, hydroentangling or thermal bonding, through to winding and slitting the roll. A person who has it holds basis weight, width and bond strength across the roll and reads the scanner's profile to correct it.
skills.learned: On the job at a nonwovens plant.

skills.name: Tufting Machine Operation
skills.what: Running a tufting machine that stitches yarn through a primary backing to make carpet and rugs: creeling and threading yarn, changing needles, hooks and knives, splicing backing and inspecting the face as it comes off. A person who has it keeps the machine on style and catches a missing row, streak or mistuft before a roll is lost.
skills.learned: On the job in a carpet mill, often starting as a creeler or tufting assistant.

skills.name: Warp Preparation
skills.what: Getting yarn ready for the loom: warping ends from a creel onto a beam at even tension, sizing the warp on a slasher, and drawing it in through drop wires, heddles and reed or tying a new warp onto the old one. A person who has it builds a beam with no crossed, slack or missing ends, in the order the style calls for.
skills.learned: On the job in a weaving mill, usually as a creeler or warper before weaving.
tools: Creels and section or direct warpers

skills.name: Textile Dyeing
skills.what: Dyeing fiber, yarn, fabric, carpet or garments in batch machines (jet, beam, package, beck, jigger) or on continuous ranges: loading, weighing dyes and chemicals to the recipe, running the cycle's temperatures and additions, and checking shade before unloading. A person who has it brings a lot to shade the first time and knows how to make a correcting add without spoiling the lot.
skills.learned: On the job in a dye house.
tools: Jet, beam and package dyeing machines

skills.name: Textile Finishing
skills.what: Giving fabric its final width, weight, hand and performance after it is woven, knit or dyed: running tenter frames, dryers, compactors, calenders, napping and shearing machines, and applying chemical finishes, coatings or a carpet backing. A person who has it sets temperature, speed, overfeed and pickup to hit the finished spec and checks width, skew and shrinkage as the fabric runs.
skills.learned: On the job in a finishing plant.

skills.name: Dye Recipe Formulation
skills.what: Working out the recipe that dyes a substrate to a customer's standard: measuring the standard on a spectrophotometer, formulating from the dye database, dyeing and correcting lab dips until they pass in tolerance and in the light booth, and scaling the recipe to the production machine. A person who has it gets a lab dip approved in few rounds and predicts how the shade will move in production.
skills.learned: On the job in a dye house color laboratory, usually after time as a dyer or laboratory technician. England's Technical Dyer and Colourist apprenticeship standard describes the same work.

skills.name: Engineering Change Management
skills.what: Carrying a change to a released design through to the floor: the change request, order or notice, its review and approval, and the update of drawing, bill of materials, work instructions and stock. A person who has it says what changes and why, names every document and part affected, sets the date the change takes effect and what happens to parts on hand, and closes it only when the floor builds to the new revision.
skills.learned: On the job in engineering, manufacturing engineering or quality, on the company's change process; configuration management courses.
tools: Redlined drawings and bills of material

skills.name: Marker Making
skills.what: Laying out every piece of every size of an order into a marker for the cutting room, by hand or with nesting software, keeping grainlines, nap and plaid repeats, and making it as short as the fabric allows. A person who has it makes markers that beat the costed efficiency and cut without a missing piece.
skills.learned: On the job in a cutting or pattern room.

skills.name: Pattern Grading
skills.what: Making each size of a pattern from the base size by grade rules: moving points by the grade increments, keeping joining seams the same length, and checking the graded nest. A person who has it grades a style across its size range so every size fits the same way.
skills.learned: On the job in a pattern room; apparel programs teach it.

skills.name: Garment Fit Evaluation
skills.what: Judging how a sample fits on a form or a fit model and measuring it against the spec: finding the cause of a pull, gape or twist and deciding the pattern correction. A person who has it runs a fit session, writes the comments and corrects the pattern so the next sample fits.
skills.learned: Technical design programs; on the job with a senior patternmaker or technical designer.

skills.name: Pattern Drafting
skills.what: Making the patterns a sewn product is cut from: drafting flat patterns from measurements, sketches or a block, by hand or on pattern CAD, with seam allowances, notches, grainlines and labels, and correcting them after a fitting. A person who has it makes a production pattern that sews together without forcing and measures to the spec.
skills.learned: Apparel and technical design programs; on the job under a senior patternmaker.

skills.name: Materials Selection
skills.what: Choosing the material and its form for a part from what the part must bear: load, temperature, environment, weight, cost and the process that will make it. A person who has it narrows the candidates by property, checks them against the environment and the manufacturing route, and names the material, its condition and its specification on the drawing.
skills.learned: Taught in the materials science and mechanical design courses of an engineering degree, and deepened on the job against a company's approved materials list.

skills.name: Design Controls
skills.what: Running a medical device's development under design controls: user needs and design inputs traced to outputs, design reviews, verification, validation and transfer, recorded in the design history file, as the FDA's quality system regulation (21 CFR 820, which now incorporates ISO 13485) requires. A person who has it keeps a project's records so each requirement traces to the test that proved it.
skills.learned: On the job in medical device engineering; courses on 21 CFR 820 and ISO 13485.

skills.name: Medical Device Risk Management
skills.what: Analyzing and controlling a medical device's risks to ISO 14971: identifying hazards and hazardous situations, estimating severity and probability, choosing controls, verifying them and keeping the risk management file through the device's life. A person who has it can show an auditor why each remaining risk is acceptable.
skills.learned: On the job in medical device engineering and quality; ISO 14971 courses.

skills.name: Reliability Prediction
skills.what: Estimating how often a design will fail before it is built or fielded: a prediction from its parts and the stress on them, a block diagram of what must work for the system to work, and the system's target shared out among its parts. A person who has it builds the model from the bill of materials and the conditions of use, states its assumptions, and corrects it with test and field data.
skills.learned: In reliability engineering courses and on a programme; the American Society for Quality's Certified Reliability Engineer covers it.

skills.name: Structural Hand Calculations
skills.what: Sizing a part by calculation before, or beside, a computer model: the free-body diagram, the load path, beam, plate and shell formulas, bolted and welded joints, buckling and the margin left. A person who has it gets to a thickness or a fastener size on paper, knows which formula's assumptions hold and uses the result to catch a finite element answer that is wrong.
skills.learned: Taught in every mechanical and aerospace engineering degree (statics, mechanics of materials, machine design) and made a habit on the job under a senior engineer's review.

skills.name: Computational Fluid Dynamics
skills.what: Predicting how a gas or a liquid flows and carries heat around or through a part with a computer model. A person who has it prepares the geometry and the mesh, sets boundary conditions that match the real case, runs the solver and checks the answer against a hand estimate or a test.
skills.learned: A fluid mechanics course and usually a graduate course in numerical methods; then on the job, correlating models to wind tunnel, flow bench or flight data.
tools: Wind tunnel and flow test data

skills.name: Mass Properties Control
skills.what: Estimating and tracking a vehicle's weight and center of gravity while it is designed and built: the weight estimate by system, its margins, a report after each design change, and weighing or inclining to confirm. A person who has it catches the change that would put the design over its weight or out of balance.
skills.learned: On the job in a shipyard's or an aircraft maker's weight group; the Society of Allied Weight Engineers trains and publishes the practice.

skills.name: Ship Stability and Hydrostatics
skills.what: Working out how a hull floats and stays upright: hydrostatics, intact and damaged stability, trim and freeboard from the hull form and the weight estimate, against the rules the ship is built to; and planning and reading the inclining experiment that proves it. A person who has it can say whether a design change keeps the ship within its stability criteria.
skills.learned: A naval architecture degree (Webb Institute, the University of Michigan, Virginia Tech, the U.S. Naval Academy and others), then a shipyard's naval architecture group; the Society of Naval Architects and Marine Engineers publishes the methods.

skills.name: Board Bring-Up
skills.what: Taking a newly built board from first power-on to working: checking rails, clocks and resets, loading the first firmware, and finding what is wrong with the design or the build. A person who has it can bring up an unfamiliar board methodically and say what to change in the next revision.
skills.learned: On the job beside the board's designer.
tools: Bench power supplies and electronic loads

skills.name: Wire Harness Design
skills.what: Designing the wiring that joins a product's electrical boxes: the wiring diagram and wire list, wire gauge and type for the current and the environment, connectors, contacts and backshells, shielding and grounding, and the routed lengths and breakouts the harness shop builds to. A person who has it produces a harness drawing and formboard a builder can work from and a design that can be installed and serviced where it has to go.
skills.learned: On the job in an electrical or harness design group; the build standard it is designed to (IPC/WHMA-A-620) is taught and certified, the design is not.

skills.name: Power Converter Design
skills.what: Designing switching power converters: choosing the topology, the magnetics and the switches, closing the control loop, and proving efficiency, regulation and thermal margin on the bench. A person who has it can take a DC-DC or AC-DC stage from a specification to tested hardware.
skills.learned: A power electronics course, then on the job with a simulator and a bench.

skills.name: Signal and Power Integrity Analysis
skills.what: Making sure fast signals arrive clean and supply rails stay quiet on a board: impedance, loss, crosstalk and timing of the channels, and the impedance and decoupling of the power network, by simulation and by measurement. A person who has it can set the stack-up and routing rules for an interface and show the built board meets them.
skills.learned: A signal integrity course, then on the job with a simulator and a high-bandwidth scope.

skills.name: Factory Layout
skills.what: Laying out a factory, a line or a cell: where stations, machines, aisles, storage and utilities go so that material and people move the shortest way and the rate can be made. A person who has it draws the layout to scale, checks flow, clearances and reach, and changes it as the product or the rate changes.
skills.learned: Taught in industrial and manufacturing engineering degrees (facilities planning) and learned on a line move or a new line. Shown by a layout that was built and made its rate.

skills.name: Equipment Specification
skills.what: Writing down what a machine, a line or a test station must do before it is bought: the rate, the process it runs, the utilities and footprint, the safety and data requirements and what it must show at acceptance; then choosing among suppliers' proposals. A person who has it writes a specification a supplier can quote and be held to, compares the quotations on the same terms and makes the case for the money.
skills.learned: On the job, on a first equipment purchase beside an experienced manufacturing or equipment engineer; no course or credential names it.
tools: Equipment specifications and statements of work

skills.name: Truss Layout
skills.what: Laying out a building's roof and floor trusses from its architectural plans in truss design software: bearings, girders, hip and valley sets, overhangs and openings. A person who has it reads the plans for every condition that changes a truss, and produces the placement plan the builder sets the trusses by.
skills.learned: On the job at a truss plant, with the Structural Building Components Association's Truss Technician Training.

skills.name: Truss Design
skills.what: Designing each truss for its loads (dead, live, snow and wind under the building code and ASCE 7) to the ANSI/TPI 1 standard in truss design software, choosing members, lumber grades and plates. A person who has it checks the software's results, resolves members that fail, and sends the plant its cutting and table files.
skills.learned: Years as a truss technician; the Structural Building Components Association's Truss Technician Training, Levels I and II.
tools: Building codes and ASCE 7 load tables

skills.name: Truss Repair Design
skills.what: Designing repairs for trusses that were damaged, cut or built wrong, and the permanent bracing a truss system needs. A person who has it specifies a repair the field crew can make and the engineer will seal.
skills.learned: Experienced truss technicians; the Structural Building Components Association's Truss Technician Training Level III.

skills.name: Trade Studies
skills.what: Choosing between ways of meeting a requirement by setting them side by side: the options, the measures that matter (mass, cost, power, risk, schedule), their weights, the numbers for each and the choice that follows, written so another engineer can check it. A person who has it frames the question before the answer, puts numbers where opinions were and says how far an input can move before the choice changes.
skills.learned: Taught in systems engineering and capstone design courses and in INCOSE's handbook; learned on the job in concept and preliminary design.

skills.name: Interface Control
skills.what: Defining where two parts of a system meet and keeping both sides to it: the mechanical envelope and mounting, the connectors and pin-outs, power, data and timing, written in an interface control document that both owners sign and that changes only by agreement. A person who has it finds the interfaces nobody owns, writes them down to the pin and catches a change on one side before it breaks the other.
skills.learned: On the job on a multi-team product; systems engineering courses and INCOSE's handbook teach the practice.
tools: Interface block diagrams and N-squared charts

skills.name: Model-Based Systems Engineering
skills.what: Describing a system in one connected model in place of separate documents: its requirements, structure, behaviour and interfaces as linked diagrams, so that a change in one place shows everywhere it matters. A person who has it builds block, activity and sequence diagrams that engineers of other disciplines can read, ties each to a requirement and keeps the model the place the design is decided.
skills.learned: Taught in systems engineering degrees and short courses; the OMG Certified Systems Modeling Professional credential tests the modeling language.

skills.name: Polishing and Buffing
skills.what: Bringing a metal surface to a specified finish, from satin to mirror, with abrasive belts, wheels, buffs and compounds: choosing the sequence of grits, holding the part so edges and features stay sharp, and checking finish and size. A person who has it polishes implants, instruments, jewelry or hardware to the finish called for without overheating, rounding or rippling the surface.
skills.learned: On the job; implant and jewelry makers train polishers for months.

skills.name: Lumber Sorting and Stacking
skills.what: Running the sorter and stacker that drop lumber into bins by grade and length and build stickered or solid packages. A person who has it keeps the sorter from jamming, places stickers straight for drying, and bands and tags packages correctly.
skills.learned: On the job in the first weeks at a sawmill.

skills.name: Edging and Trimming
skills.what: Edging, resawing and trimming boards to width and length for the most value, at edger, gang, resaw and trimmer stations and their optimizers. A person who has it checks the optimizer's decision against what the board shows, and corrects the solution when the scan is wrong.
skills.learned: On the job in a sawmill.

skills.name: Log Breakdown Sawing
skills.what: Sawing logs into cants, boards and flitches on a head rig, canter or twin band, usually from a booth with a scanner and optimizer. A person who has it turns and positions each log for the most value, watches saw deviation and feed, and stops the line before a bad saw ruins lumber.
skills.learned: On the job, after years at the lower stations of a sawmill; sawmill equipment makers train sawyers on their optimizers.

skills.name: Saw Grinding
skills.what: Sharpening band and circular saws on automatic grinders to the tooth profile, hook and clearance angles the cut needs. A person who has it sets up the grinder for each saw, dresses the wheel to the profile, and checks the teeth for burn, even height and gullet shape.
skills.learned: In a sawmill filing room, as a filer's helper or apprentice.
tools: Automatic band and circular saw grinders

skills.name: Saw Swaging and Shaping
skills.what: Spreading each tooth tip of a band saw with a swage and shaping it to an even kerf on both sides. A person who has it sets the swage and shaper, measures the kerf on every tooth, and keeps the saw cutting straight.
skills.learned: In a filing room, as part of a filer apprenticeship.

skills.name: Saw Tipping
skills.what: Putting hard tips on saw teeth, by welding stellite on band saw teeth or brazing carbide tips on circular saws, then grinding them to profile. A person who has it tips evenly so every tooth cuts, and replaces a broken tip without overheating the plate.
skills.learned: In a filing room; on the job.

skills.name: Band Saw Benching
skills.what: Bringing a band saw blade flat, tensioned and straight-backed on the bench: rolling tension into it with a stretcher roll, leveling bumps and twists with hammers, checking it with straightedges and tension gauges, and repairing cracks. A person who has it reads from the blade how the saw ran in the mill, and benches it to cut straight at speed.
skills.learned: Years in a filing room under a head filer, through a filer apprenticeship; British Columbia trains and certifies saw filers and benchpersons as a trade.

skills.name: Circular Saw Benching
skills.what: Leveling and tensioning circular saw plates so they stay flat and stable at speed: hammering or rolling tension, and checking flatness and run-out on the anvil and arbor. A person who has it tensions each saw for its speed and diameter, and diagnoses wobble and heating from how it cut.
skills.learned: Years in a filing room; part of a saw filer apprenticeship.

skills.name: Stationary Woodworking Machine Operation
skills.what: Setting up and using the basic machines of a wood shop safely: table saw, jointer, thickness planer, band saw, drill press and shaper. A person who has it sets fences, heights and guards, feeds stock without kickback, and cuts parts square and to size.
skills.learned: Woodworking programs at high schools and community colleges, and on the job; the Woodwork Career Alliance credentials woodworkers machine by machine.

skills.name: CNC Router Operation
skills.what: Running a CNC router that cuts, bores and shapes parts from sheet goods and solid wood (wood panels, plastics, composite panels and aluminum): loading the nest, setting the vacuum hold-down and spoilboard, choosing, changing and measuring tools, and checking first parts. A person who has it keeps small parts from moving, chooses feeds that leave clean edges without melting or chipping, and resurfaces the spoilboard when it is worn.
skills.learned: Woodworking and CNC programs at community colleges, and on the job in cabinet, furniture, sign and plastics shops; the Woodwork Career Alliance has a CNC router credential.
tools: Router bits, compression cutters and drills

skills.name: Edgebanding
skills.what: Applying edgebanding to panel parts on an edgebander: gluing, end trimming, flush and radius trimming, scraping and buffing. A person who has it sets the machine for each band's thickness and material, holds glue line and trim quality, and changes over between colors quickly.
skills.learned: On the job in a cabinet or furniture plant; the Woodwork Career Alliance has an edgebander credential.
tools: Hot melt and PUR glue pots

skills.name: Panel Saw Operation
skills.what: Cutting sheet goods (plywood, particleboard, MDF and laminated panels) into parts from an optimized cut list, on a beam saw, sliding table saw or vertical panel saw. A person who has it loads the cutting pattern, keeps laminated faces chip-free, and labels and stacks parts for the next machine.
skills.learned: On the job in a cabinet, furniture or panel plant.

skills.name: Planer and Moulder Setup
skills.what: Setting up and running planers and moulders that surface and profile lumber and millwork: grinding and jointing knives, setting heads, pressure and feed rolls, and checking the profile against its template. A person who has it changes over to a new profile and holds size and surface at speed.
skills.learned: On the job in a planer mill or millwork plant; knife grinding is often learned from the moulder's maker.

skills.name: Wide-Belt Sanding
skills.what: Sanding panels, doors and parts flat and to thickness on a wide-belt sander. A person who has it chooses the belts and grit sequence, sets heads, platens and feed speed, and finds the cause of chatter marks, burns and snipe.
skills.learned: On the job in a panel, cabinet or millwork plant.

skills.name: Brazer Performance Qualification
skills.what: Passing a brazing test to a code: brazing test joints in the set process, position and joint type, which then pass peel, section or bend examination. A person who has it is qualified for that range of joints, and keeps the qualification current by brazing.
skills.learned: Tested to ASME Section IX, Part QB, or AWS B2.2, at the employer or a test facility.

skills.name: Ship Structural Layout
skills.what: Laying out ship structure from the drawings and the loft data: marking the reference lines a hull is built to (centerline, frame, waterline and buttock lines) and the place of plates, stiffeners, brackets and cutouts on a panel or unit. A person who has it transfers the lines with tape, chalk line, level and laser, and allows for weld shrinkage and the stock left for trimming.
skills.learned: Shipfitter apprenticeships at the shipyards and on the job; shipbuilding programs at community colleges near the yards.

skills.name: Hull Structure Fit-Up
skills.what: Fitting plate, frames, stiffeners and bulkheads into panels, units and blocks, and landing one block on another at erection. A person who has it pulls the parts to the lines with dogs, wedges, jacks and come-alongs, holds the gap and alignment the welding procedure calls for, and tacks them so they stay.
skills.learned: Shipfitter apprenticeships (four years at the large yards) and on the job.

skills.name: Flame Straightening
skills.what: Taking distortion out of welded plate and structure with controlled heat: spot, line and vee heats, with restraint or a water quench where the steel allows it. A person who has it reads the distortion, chooses the heat pattern, stays within the temperature limit of the metal and checks flatness and fairness after.
skills.learned: On the job in shipyards and structural shops, from experienced fitters; the Federal Highway Administration's guide to heat-straightening steel is the usual written reference.

skills.name: Cold Heading
skills.what: Forming fasteners and small parts from wire at room temperature on single-die headers and multi-station cold formers: straightening and feeding the wire, cutting off, upsetting, extruding and piercing station by station, and setting the transfer fingers and tooling. A person who has it sets a header up from a stripped machine to good parts, and changes broken tooling without crashing it.
skills.learned: On the job in a fastener plant, from operator to setup. Machine makers train on their own formers.
tools: Single-die headers and multi-station cold formers
Header dies, punches and transfer fingers

skills.name: Forging Die Setup
skills.what: Setting forging dies in a hammer, press or upsetter: preheating the dies, aligning and clamping them to the die match and shut height, setting stroke, transfer and spray, and forging first pieces until they pass. A person who has it reads the die drawing and corrects a mismatch with the right adjustment.
skills.learned: On the job in a forge shop after time as an operator.

skills.name: Impression-Die Forging
skills.what: Forging parts in shaped dies on a hammer, press or upsetter: heating the bar by furnace or induction, running preform, blocker and finisher impressions, lubricating the dies, trimming the flash and checking the forging. A person who has it keeps the stock at temperature, sees underfill and laps in the part, and knows when a die is wearing out.
skills.learned: On the job in a closed-die forge shop.
tools: Forging hammers, mechanical and screw presses and upsetters

skills.name: Open-Die Forging
skills.what: Working a heated billet or ingot between flat or simple dies on a hammer or press, with a manipulator or by hand: upsetting, drawing out, punching and saddle work to a forging drawing, reheating as needed. A person who has it plans the sequence of blows from the drawing, measures the hot part as it goes, and finishes at forging temperature.
skills.learned: On the job beside a hammersmith or press operator. The Forging Industry Association's Forging University runs courses online.
tools: Flat, V and swage dies and saddles

skills.name: Thread Rolling
skills.what: Rolling threads onto blanks between flat or cylindrical dies: setting die match and penetration, feeding the blanks, and checking pitch diameter and thread form. A person who has it sets a roller so the thread starts true and the dies last.
skills.learned: On the job in a fastener or turned-parts plant.

skills.name: Ring Rolling
skills.what: Making seamless rings: upsetting and punching a hot preform, then rolling it out on a radial-axial ring mill to diameter, height and wall, and checking it to the drawing. A person who has it runs the mill so the ring grows round without dishing or fishtails.
skills.learned: On the job in an open-die and ring rolling forge, after years on the hammer or press. The Forging Industry Association runs ring rolling training.

skills.name: Aluminum Extrusion
skills.what: Running an aluminum extrusion press: heating billets, changing and preheating dies, setting ram speed and container and exit temperatures, taking the profile on the puller through the quench, stretching it straight, sawing it to length, and checking the profile's size and surface. A person who has it spots a failing die or a tearing profile, and changes dies fast enough to keep the press running.
skills.learned: On the job on a press crew. Aluminum Extrusion Press Operator became a registered apprenticeship in 2024 (4,000 hours).

skills.name: Cold Rolling
skills.what: Reducing coiled strip to final gauge, temper and flatness at room temperature on a reversing, tandem or temper mill: threading the coil, setting reduction and tension, controlling gauge and shape, managing roll coolant and inspecting the surface. A person who has it changes work rolls before they mark the strip, and knows which defects come from the mill and which came with the coil.
skills.learned: On the job in a cold mill or an aluminum rolling mill.

skills.name: Hot Rolling
skills.what: Rolling heated slabs, blooms or billets down to plate, strip, bar or rod: discharging from the reheat furnace, descaling, running the roughing and finishing stands to the pass schedule, controlling gauge, width and temperature, and coiling or cooling the product. A person who has it reads the mill's screens and the bar itself, clears a cobble safely, and keeps the product within size and surface limits.
skills.learned: On the job on a hot mill crew, from the floor to the pulpit.

skills.name: Roll Forming
skills.what: Bending coil into a long profile through a series of roll stands: threading the line, setting the roll tooling stand by stand, running the in-line punching and cut-off, and checking profile and length. A person who has it fixes bow, twist, flare and edge wave at the stand that causes them.
skills.learned: On the job at a roll forming plant. Line makers train on their tooling.
tools: Roll forming lines and roll tooling

skills.name: Rolling Mill Setup
skills.what: Getting a rolling mill ready for the next product: changing work and backup rolls, setting roll gaps, guides and pass lines, zeroing the stands, and proving the setup on the first bars or coils. A person who has it works from the roll and guide schedule, and fixes a product that is twisting, cobbling or off size at the stand that causes it.
skills.learned: On the job in a rolling mill after time as an operator. Roll shops train the roll changers.

skills.name: Welded Tube Mill Operation
skills.what: Making welded pipe and tube from strip on a tube mill: forming it through the roll stands, welding the seam by high-frequency induction or resistance, scarfing the bead, sizing, straightening, cutting to length and testing the weld. A person who has it sets weld power and squeeze to the gauge and speed, and catches a bad weld before it reaches the cut-off.
skills.learned: On the job at a pipe and tube mill.
tools: Tube mills with forming and sizing stands

skills.name: Stranding and Cabling
skills.what: Twisting wires into stranded conductors, and insulated conductors into cables, on stranders, bunchers and cablers: setting lay length and direction and payoff and take-up tension, and adding fillers, binders, tapes and shields. A person who has it checks diameter, lay and strand count and keeps the reel winding clean.
skills.learned: On the job at a wire and cable plant.

skills.name: Wire Drawing
skills.what: Drawing steel, copper or aluminum rod and wire down to size through a series of dies on single-block or multiwire machines: setting the die schedule, pointing and stringing up, keeping lubricant, cooling and the inline annealer right, and welding in a new rod or a break. A person who has it checks diameter, surface, temper and elongation coil by coil, and finds why wire is breaking and which die is worn.
skills.learned: On the job at a wire mill or a wire and cable plant; the Wire Association International teaches wire drawing and dies.
tools: Rod breakdown, multiwire and single-block drawing machines

skills.name: Molten Metal Sampling
skills.what: Taking the temperature and a chemistry sample from a furnace, ladle or tundish with immersion probes, and getting the sample to the spectrometer. A person who has it dips at the right depth and for the right time, tells a bad probe reading from a good one and labels each sample to its heat.
skills.learned: On the job in the first weeks on a melt deck or a caster crew.

skills.name: Continuous Casting
skills.what: Running a continuous caster that turns liquid steel into slabs, blooms or billets: preparing and preheating the tundish, opening the ladle, starting the strand on the dummy bar, holding mold level, casting speed, mold powder and secondary cooling, cutting to length, and changing tundishes in sequence. A person who has it watches for the signs of a breakout and acts before the shell tears.
skills.learned: On the job on a caster crew, from the floor to the pulpit.
tools: Mold level and breakout detection systems

skills.name: Direct Chill Casting
skills.what: Casting aluminum sheet ingot or extrusion billet in a direct-chill casting pit: preparing the table and molds, filtering and degassing the metal on the way, starting the drop, holding water flow and casting speed, then sawing and stacking. A person who has it knows a cast fails at the start or the end of a drop, and inspects for cracks and bleed-outs.
skills.learned: On the job in an aluminum casthouse at a rolling mill, an extrusion plant or a smelter.

skills.name: Ductile Iron Treatment
skills.what: Turning molten iron into ductile iron in the ladle: adding magnesium alloy by sandwich, cover-ladle or wire-feed treatment, inoculating, and getting the iron poured before the treatment fades. A person who has it weighs the treatment to the iron's weight and sulfur, checks the result by chill wedge, thermal analysis or sample, and knows what a faded ladle does to the castings.
skills.learned: On the job in an iron foundry. The American Foundry Society's institute teaches iron melting and treatment.

skills.name: Electric Arc Furnace Operation
skills.what: Melting scrap and direct-reduced iron in an electric arc furnace and bringing the heat to tap: charging by bucket, boring in, running the power program, foaming the slag with carbon and oxygen, deslagging, and tapping into the ladle at the aim chemistry and temperature. A person who has it reads the arc, the slag and the furnace's water and lining condition, and keeps tap-to-tap time down without risking a breakout.
skills.learned: On the job in an electric steel melt shop, from furnace helper to first helper and melter. The Association for Iron & Steel Technology runs steelmaking courses.
tools: Electric arc furnaces and their pulpit controls
Oxygen and carbon injection lances and burners

skills.name: Furnace and Ladle Refractory Maintenance
skills.what: Keeping the refractory linings of melting furnaces, ladles and tundishes fit to hold metal: inspecting between heats, gunning and patching, ramming and sintering a new induction lining, and preparing and preheating ladles and tundishes. A person who has it judges how much lining is left, dries every repair before metal touches it, and takes a ladle out of service before it burns through.
skills.learned: On the job in a melt shop or foundry. Refractory makers train crews on their materials.

skills.name: Induction Furnace Melting
skills.what: Melting iron, steel or nonferrous charge in a coreless induction furnace: working out and weighing the charge, melting down, skimming slag, sampling and correcting the chemistry, superheating and tapping into ladles. A person who has it watches power and lining wear, knows the signs of a lining about to fail, and never charges wet or sealed scrap.
skills.learned: On the job on a foundry melt deck. The American Foundry Society's institute runs melting courses, and furnace makers train on their own power supplies.
tools: Coreless induction furnaces and power supplies
Lining wear and ground leak detectors

skills.name: Ladle Metallurgy
skills.what: Finishing a heat of steel in the ladle furnace before it goes to the caster: alloying to the aim chemistry, building the slag to take out sulfur, stirring with argon, feeding calcium or alloy wire, heating to the caster's schedule, and vacuum degassing where the grade needs it. A person who has it delivers the heat on chemistry, on temperature and on time for the sequence, and knows what each addition does to cleanliness.
skills.learned: Years in a melt shop, then training on the ladle furnace pulpit. The mill's metallurgists teach the grade practices.

skills.name: Foundry Sand Control
skills.what: Keeping molding sand right: mulling return sand with clay, water and additives, testing its compactability, moisture, permeability and strength, and adjusting the mix. For chemically bonded sand, it means reclaiming the sand and holding binder ratio and work time. A person who has it traces a run of casting defects back to the sand.
skills.learned: On the job at a foundry's muller and sand laboratory. The American Foundry Society publishes the sand test methods and teaches them.

skills.name: Automatic Molding Line Operation
skills.what: Running an automatic foundry molding machine and its line: setting the pattern plates, squeeze and blow, setting cores, closing the molds, conveying them to pour and cooling, and running the shakeout. A person who has it keeps the line at rate, keeps the molds hard, square and free of crush, and changes patterns quickly.
skills.learned: On the job in a production foundry. Machine makers train on their own lines.
tools: Flaskless vertical and horizontal molding machines

skills.name: Casting Grinding
skills.what: Grinding castings clean after shakeout and cut-off: taking riser and gate contacts down to the contour, removing fins and burnt-on sand, and blending repairs, with portable, swing-frame and stand grinders or a robotic cell. A person who has it grinds to the casting's surface without gouging it, and leaves the finish the customer calls for.
skills.learned: On the job in a foundry cleaning room.

skills.name: Casting Weld Repair
skills.what: Repairing defects in castings by welding: excavating the defect that inspection found, by arc-air or grinding; preheating; welding the cavity to the qualified procedure; post-heating and grinding back; and sending it for re-inspection. A person who has it is qualified to the casting specification, and keeps the repair map the customer asks for.
skills.learned: On the job in a steel or iron foundry. Welders and procedures for steel castings qualify to ASTM A488 or ASME Section IX.
tools: Stick, flux-cored and TIG welding machines

skills.name: Gating and Riser Design
skills.what: Designing how metal enters and feeds a casting: sizing sprues, runners, gates, risers and chills, and proving the design by simulating fill and solidification before a pattern is made. A person who has it reads a simulation for misruns, cold shuts and shrinkage, and moves the feeding until the casting is sound.
skills.learned: University metallurgy and casting courses. The American Foundry Society and the software makers teach gating and simulation.

skills.name: Resin Drying and Handling
skills.what: Getting plastic resin to the machine dry, clean and in the right blend: running desiccant and hot-air dryers to the material's time and dew point, vacuum loaders and blenders, and returning regrind at its allowed ratio.
